SOAH DOCKET NO. 473-26-16349
PUC DOCKET NO. 59475
JOINT APPLICATION OF ONCOR ELECTRIC DELIVERY COMPANY LLC AND LCRA TRANSMISSION SERVICES CORPORATION TO AMEND THEIR CERTIFICATES OF CONVENIENCE AND NECESSITY FOR THE BELL COUNTY EAST SWITCH TO BIG HILL SUBSTATION 765-KV TRANSMISSION LINE PROJECT
BEFORE THE STATE OFFICE OF ADMINISTRATIVE HEARINGS
INTERVENOR NELDA HOWTON’S COMBINED REPLY TO APPLICANTS’ AND COMMISSION STAFF’S BRIEFS ON REMANDED PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUE NOS. 11 AND 13
TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:
Intervenor Nelda Howton, appearing pro se, submits this combined response under SOAH Order No. 35. She responds to Applicants’ position as described in their Directory of Evidence and to Commission Staff’s Initial Brief on Remand, filed October 7, 2026 (PUC Interchange Item No. 6631). This reply is confined to Preliminary Order Issue Nos. 11 and 13 and relies on the existing evidentiary record; it does not request that the administrative law judges reopen that record.¹
I. SUMMARY OF POSITION
Mrs. Howton does not dispute that Texas needs reliable electric service or that ERCOT may identify regional transmission deficiencies. The question on remand is narrower: whether these particular proposed facilities have been proved necessary to satisfy a state or federal reliability standard and what consumer congestion-cost savings these facilities are estimated to produce. A recommendation in a large regional plan is not equivalent to proof that every individual line within the plan must be built.
As a private landowner whose community has already endured extraordinary damage and rebuilding, Mrs. Howton asks that the evidence be measured carefully before another lasting burden is imposed on Texas families. Her position is that the applications should be denied for failure to establish the project-specific need asked about in Issue No. 11. If the Commission nonetheless approves a route, her separately stated alternative preference remains Route 296 as it serves a “Need” rather than a route using Link F20; routing, even though it is not the issue now remanded.
II. ISSUE NO. 11: THE REQUIRED PROJECT-SPECIFIC SHOWING HAS NOT BEEN MADE
Issue No. 11 asks: “Are the proposed transmission facilities necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards?”² Staff answers yes because the projects, “in conjunction with other” Permian Basin Reliability Plan projects, would resolve reliability criteria violations under NERC TPL-001-5.1 and ERCOT planning criteria.³ But proving that a collection of improvements can correct a modeled system deficiency is not the same as proving the necessity of the Bell County East–Big Hill facilities themselves.
Staff cites ERCOT’s steady-state and dynamic studies and the 2024 and 2025 Regional Transmission Plans, then adopts Applicants’ conclusion that Import Path 2 qualifies as a reliability project under 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii).⁴ The missing step is a project-specific demonstration: what identified standard violation persists in the absence of these facilities, in what relevant study year and scenario, and why a different remedy would not address it? The ALJs should distinguish the reliability of ERCOT’s planning methodology from the legal conclusion that this precise certificate amendment is necessary.
The existing record also reflects significant uncertainty in the forecasts used to justify the preferred infrastructure. The Proposal for Decision’s Finding of Fact No. 92, as identified in another intervenor’s October 7 brief, addresses at least 3,571 MW removed from the Permian Basin Reliability Plan’s non-oil-and-gas load under ERCOT’s adjusted forecasting method.⁵ That change deserves evaluation against the projected need for Import Path 2 rather than assuming earlier planning conclusions remain unchanged. Mrs. Howton does not claim that a forecast correction by itself proves no transmission is required; she submits that the Commission cannot overlook its impact on the burden of proof.
Applicants’ own cited statement that later planning models “assume that the Import Path 2 Projects are in service” underscores the problem.⁶ Modeling a facility as already present may show how a selected configuration performs; without a meaningful counterfactual, it does not alone establish the facility’s indispensable role. The Commission should avoid circular reasoning: a project cannot be deemed mandatory merely because an analysis of the preferred plan includes it.
A further distinction concerns federal requirements. The Federal Power Act’s definition of a “reliability standard” expressly excludes “any requirement to enlarge such facilities or to construct new transmission capacity or generation capacity.” 16 U.S.C. § 824o(a)(3). This provision does not eliminate the obligation to remedy reliability deficiencies, but it defeats any suggestion that citation to a NERC planning standard alone mandates construction of this exact 765-kV project. The particular remedy still requires evidentiary support.
Likewise, the Commission must make the necessity determination under PURA § 37.056, not merely ratify a planning preference. ERCOT’s expert role deserves weight, but independent regulatory judgment remains necessary, especially when record findings call major load assumptions into question. Mrs. Howton urges the ALJs to find Issue No. 11 not established for these particular facilities on the presently cited proof.
III. BELL COUNTY LOAD GROWTH, GENERATION ASSUMPTIONS, AND THE EASTERN TERMINUS
The Applicants characterize this proposed line as part of a means to move additional power toward the Permian Basin. Mrs. Howton asks a corresponding, project-specific question: what load and power-flow assumptions establish that sufficient electricity can be delivered through the Bell County East endpoint while reliably serving rapidly expanding electricity requirements in Bell County? A transmission facility conveys power; it does not create generating capacity. Electricity need not be generated within Bell County to reach the proposed line, because the endpoint is part of an interconnected grid. The relevant evidentiary issue is whether generation dispatch, available transmission capacity, local demand, and projected imports were adequately reflected in the relied-upon planning cases.
Publicly announced Bell County data-center development illustrates why these assumptions warrant scrutiny. Rowan Digital Infrastructure announced in January 2026 that construction had begun on its 300-MW Project Temple campus, with operations anticipated in 2027 and power arrangements developed with Oncor. Rowan separately lists Project Ranger among its approved or proposed Temple buildings. Meta has publicly reported its Temple data-center operations. Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation project records list an Oppidan-owned 5-MW Temple data-center construction project at 2313 Eberhardt Road. An earlier Rowan Moriah/Temple Green campus was announced at a substantially larger planned capacity, but reporting indicates that its prior tenant vacated the property and that repurposing was contemplated; its announced capacity cannot responsibly be treated as a current, additive electrical load. These are public project descriptions, NOT findings that the facilities are all in service, have drawn their announced peak load, or were omitted from ERCOT models.
The governing test is not whether Bell County has a generating station producing the full quantity of electricity for export. Under Tex. Util. Code § 37.056(c-1) and 16 Tex. Admin. Code § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(II), historical load, forecast load growth, and additional loads seeking interconnection are relevant to the ERCOT reliability assessment, with projected growth supported by quantifiable evidence. Mrs. Howton requests a finding addressing whether the admitted record identifies (a) which Bell County large loads were included, (b) the forecast years and magnitude assumed for those loads, (c) generation and import assumptions at the Bell County East terminal, and (d) the reliability deficiency that would arise without THIS proposed line after those assumptions are applied. Those questions are not answered simply by pointing to system-wide Permian Basin needs.
Mrs. Howton does not assert that new press reports are admitted hearing evidence or that they establish a statutory violation by Applicants. The above public information is offered only to explain the specificity of the existing-record inquiry. The ALJs should rest their remand findings on admitted evidence and should not infer either that Bell County lacks access to grid power or that publicly announced data-center capacities represent verified contemporaneous load. If the existing record lacks a supported answer, the ALJs should identify that evidentiary shortfall rather than fill it with assumptions.
IV. ISSUE NO. 13: STAFF’S PLAN-LEVEL FIGURES DO NOT ANSWER THE COMMISSION’S QUESTION
Issue No. 13 asks for “the estimated congestion cost savings for consumers that may result from the proposed transmission facilities,” taking current and expected future congestion into account.² Staff first maintains that this inquiry is unnecessary if the projects qualify as reliability projects; it then offers conditional economic comparisons.⁷ Whatever legal classification ultimately applies, the remand order expressly directs an answer to Issue No. 13. That answer should make clear what the present record can and cannot estimate.
Staff quotes an ERCOT comparison between comprehensive 345-kV and 765-kV transmission plans. For 2034, Staff reports estimated energy consumer costs of $18.342 billion in the base case, $18.143 billion under the 345-kV plan, and $18.279 billion under the 765-kV plan. Those figures yield respective savings of approximately $199 million and $63 million against the base case. For 2039, Staff reports $22.070 billion in the base case, $22.143 billion with the 345-kV plan, and $21.914 billion with the 765-kV plan approximately $156 million below the base case for the 765-kV plan.⁸
Those figures warrant two cautions. First, the quoted savings are estimates associated with entire alternative plans, not a separately identified estimate for the Bell County East–Big Hill project. Second, Staff’s own cited 2034 comparison shows the 345-kV plan with the greater estimated consumer savings, even though Staff favors the 765-kV plan on longer-term grounds. No one should characterize either comparison as a measured, isolated benefit delivered by these specific facilities.
Similarly, an asserted reduction in “congestion rent” across a larger transmission configuration does not, without explanation and attribution, supply the project-specific answer required by Issue No. 13.⁹ The ALJs should expressly identify the limits of the estimate, including any inability to distinguish Import Path 2 benefits from savings attributable to other facilities built in the same plan.
The relevant rule, 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(A), distinguishes economic and reliability bases for transmission need. Staff’s legal position that an independently supported reliability project need not also qualify under the economic-project test should be fairly recognized. But that is not permission to treat an incomplete reliability demonstration as established or to avoid addressing the Commission’s separately remanded consumer-savings question. If reliability status is not proved, the Commission cannot simply apply the reliability classification to bypass the otherwise applicable economic showing.
V. REGULATORY RESPONSIBILITY AND REQUESTED FINDINGS
Mrs. Howton respectfully asks the ALJs to make clear findings that (1) evidence of broad system deficiencies does not necessarily establish that this particular 765-kV segment is necessary; (2) a planning model assuming construction of Import Path 2 does not, standing alone, measure consequences of omitting it; (3) material adjustments in the underlying load forecast must be accounted for in determining the weight of the Applicants’ reliability proof; and (4) the plan-level cost comparisons presented by Staff do not, without additional attribution, provide a standalone estimate of consumer congestion savings from these proposed facilities.
The duty imposed by PURA § 37.056 is especially important when a project permanently affects private land, community investments, and utility customers who may ultimately bear project costs. Mrs. Howton does not seek a special exemption from electric-grid needs; she asks that the same statutory evidentiary protections operate before condemnation and construction follow from an approval. Her concerns regarding the proper statutory scope of regional planning and House Bill 5066 reinforce her request for careful scrutiny, but she does not ask the ALJs to resolve a new legislative-intent dispute outside Issues 11 and 13.
VI. PRAYER
WHEREFORE, PREMISES CONSIDERED, Intervenor Nelda Howton respectfully requests that the Administrative Law Judges: (1) decline to find these specific proposed transmission facilities necessary under Issue No. 11 absent an adequate, record-supported project-specific demonstration; (2) find under Issue No. 13 that the cited plan-wide economic comparisons do not furnish a distinct estimate of congestion-cost savings attributable to these facilities; (3) recommend denial of the requested certificate amendments on the evidence presently before them; and (4) grant such further relief, consistent with the limited scope of remand and the existing record, as may be appropriate.
Respectfully submitted,
/s/Nelda Howton
Nelda Howton
Intervenor Pro Se
12600 FM 2843, Salado, Texas 76571
